claim: The cranial endo and dermal skeletons evolved independently over 470 million years ago.
source: The cranial endo and dermal skeletons, which comprise the vertebrate skull, evolved independently over 470 million years ago and form separately during embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific literature on vertebrate evolution.

claim: The cranial endo and dermal skeletons form separately during embryogenesis.
source: The cranial endo and dermal skeletons, which comprise the vertebrate skull, evolved independently over 470 million years ago and form separately during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement of established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Much of the cartilaginous chondrocranium is transient in mammals, undergoing endochondral ossification or disappearing.
source: In mammals, much of the cartilaginous chondrocranium is transient, undergoing endochondral ossification or disappearing, so its role in skull morphogenesis is not well studied and it remains an enigmatic structure.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about mammalian chondrocranium development.

claim: The role of the chondrocranium in skull morphogenesis is not well studied.
source: In mammals, much of the cartilaginous chondrocranium is transient, undergoing endochondral ossification or disappearing, so its role in skull morphogenesis is not well studied and it remains an enigmatic structure.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Complete 3D reconstructions of the laboratory mouse chondrocranium from embryonic day (E) 13.5 through E17.5 were provided using a novel methodology of uncertainty-guided segmentation of phosphotungstic enhanced 3D micro-computed tomography images with sparse annotation.
source: We provide complete 3D reconstructions of the laboratory mouse chondrocranium from embryonic day (E) 13.5 through E17.5 using a novel methodology of uncertainty-guided segmentation of phosphotungstic enhanced 3D micro-computed tomography images with sparse annotation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript and the resulting data.

claim: The dermatocranium develops outside of and in shapes that conform to the chondrocranium.
source: We show that the dermatocranium develops outside of and in shapes that conform to the chondrocranium.
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from 3D reconstructions and morphological analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Fgfr2 variant has direct effects on embryonic cartilage.
source: Results reveal direct effects of the Fgfr2 variant on embryonic cartilage, on chondrocranium morphology, and on the association between chondrocranium and dermatocranium development.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and morphological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Fgfr2 variant has direct effects on chondrocranium morphology.
source: Results reveal direct effects of the Fgfr2 variant on embryonic cartilage, on chondrocranium morphology, and on the association between chondrocranium and dermatocranium development.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Fgfr2 variant has direct effects on the association between chondrocranium and dermatocranium development.
source: Results reveal direct effects of the Fgfr2 variant on embryonic cartilage, on chondrocranium morphology, and on the association between chondrocranium and dermatocranium development.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological integration analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a trend of relatively more chondrocytes, larger chondrocytes, and/or more matrix in the Fgfr2cC342Y/+ embryos at all timepoints before the chondrocranium begins to disintegrate at E16.5.
source: Histologically, we observe a trend of relatively more chondrocytes, larger chondrocytes, and/or more matrix in the Fgfr2cC342Y/+ embryos at all timepoints before the chondrocranium begins to disintegrate at E16.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data presented in Figure 3G-L.

claim: The chondrocrania and forming dermatocrania of Fgfr2cC342Y/+ embryos are relatively large.
source: The chondrocrania and forming dermatocrania of Fgfr2cC342Y/+ embryos are relatively large, but a contrasting trend begins at E16.5 and continues into early postnatal (P0 and P2) timepoints, with the skulls of older Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice reduced in most dimensions compared to Fgfr2c+/+ littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric data presented in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: A contrasting trend begins at E16.5 and continues into early postnatal (P0 and P2) timepoints, with the skulls of older Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice reduced in most dimensions compared to Fgfr2c+/+ littermates.
source: The chondrocrania and forming dermatocrania of Fgfr2cC342Y/+ embryos are relatively large, but a contrasting trend begins at E16.5 and continues into early postnatal (P0 and P2) timepoints, with the skulls of older Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice reduced in most dimensions compared to Fgfr2c+/+ littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The emergence of the cranial endoskeleton was followed by the appearance of the cranial dermal skeleton 470 Mya or earlier.
source: The emergence of the cranial endoskeleton was followed by the appearance of the cranial dermal skeleton 470 Mya or earlier (Janvier, 2015; Janvier, 1993; Sansom and Andreev, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on vertebrate evolution.

claim: The cranial endoskeleton includes the cartilaginous chondrocranium and pharyngeal skeleton that form prior to adjacent cranial dermal bones of the dermatocranium.
source: The cranial endoskeleton includes the cartilaginous chondrocranium and pharyngeal skeleton that form prior to adjacent cranial dermal bones of the dermatocranium (de Beer, 1937; Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017a; Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017b; Pitirri et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Elements of the endo and dermal skeletal systems have changed drastically over evolutionary time.
source: Though elements of these two skeletal systems have changed drastically over evolutionary time (Janvier, 1993; Schultze, 1993; Zhu et al., 2013), their association has been maintained, excepting in Chondrichthyes who secondarily lost their dermal skeleton (Schultze, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on vertebrate evolution.

claim: The association between the endo and dermal skeletal systems has been maintained over evolutionary time, excepting in Chondrichthyes who secondarily lost their dermal skeleton.
source: Though elements of these two skeletal systems have changed drastically over evolutionary time (Janvier, 1993; Schultze, 1993; Zhu et al., 2013), their association has been maintained, excepting in Chondrichthyes who secondarily lost their dermal skeleton (Schultze, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on vertebrate evolution.

claim: Most modern vertebrate skulls are composite structures formed by the union of the endo and dermal (exo) cranial skeletons that form embryonically and/or evolutionarily in cartilage and bone, respectively, and evolved as distinct systems.
source: Most modern vertebrate skulls are composite structures formed by the union of the endo and dermal (exo) cranial skeletons that form embryonically and/or evolutionarily in cartilage and bone, respectively, and evolved as distinct systems (Hirasawa and Kuratani, 2015; Jarvik, 1980; Patterson, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on vertebrate skull evolution.

claim: Chondrocranial morphology directly impacts the formation of cranial dermal bones until cartilages dissolve or are mineralized endochondrally.
source: We propose that chondrocranial morphology directly impacts the formation of cranial dermal bones until cartilages dissolve or are mineralized endochondrally.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their characterization of the mouse chondrocranium.

claim: Elements of the mouse chondrocranium form individually in sequence beginning at embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5).
source: Elements of the mouse chondrocranium form individually in sequence beginning at embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5), fuse to provide an intricate protective covering for the brain and other sense organs, and parts of these elements begin to dissolve by E16.5 (Pitirri et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Parts of chondrocranial elements begin to dissolve by E16.5.
source: Elements of the mouse chondrocranium form individually in sequence beginning at embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5), fuse to provide an intricate protective covering for the brain and other sense organs, and parts of these elements begin to dissolve by E16.5 (Pitirri et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: No modern vertebrate species has lost the chondrocranium during evolution suggesting its essential role in skull development.
source: Though many chondrocranial elements are transient, no modern vertebrate species has lost the chondrocranium during evolution suggesting its essential role in skull development (Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents an inference about the functional importance of the chondrocranium.

claim: Observed variation in chondrocranial anatomy across species indicates its contribution to phylogenetic differences in skull morphology.
source: Observed variation in chondrocranial anatomy across species (de Beer, 1937) indicates its contribution to phylogenetic differences in skull morphology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents an inference about the evolutionary significance of chondrocranial variation.

claim: Dermal bones of the skull arise individually in association with chondrocranial cartilages.
source: Dermal bones of the skull arise individually in association with chondrocranial cartilages (Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017a; Pitirri et al., 2020) but are ultimately joined with other bones by sutures that serve as essential sites of bone formation and growth (Opperman, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dermal bones are ultimately joined with other bones by sutures that serve as essential sites of bone formation and growth.
source: Dermal bones of the skull arise individually in association with chondrocranial cartilages (Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017a; Pitirri et al., 2020) but are ultimately joined with other bones by sutures that serve as essential sites of bone formation and growth (Opperman, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: During growth, mesenchyme of the suture keeps adjacent bones separated while osteoprogenitor mesenchymal cells within the osteogenic fronts of these bones proliferate and differentiate into osteoblasts that mineralize osteoid by intramembranous ossification.
source: During growth, mesenchyme of the suture keeps adjacent bones separated while osteoprogenitor mesenchymal cells within the osteogenic fronts of these bones proliferate and differentiate into osteoblasts that mineralize osteoid by intramembranous ossification (Farmer et al., 2021; Holmes et al., 2021; Iseki et al., 1997; Opperman, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on suture biology.

claim: In craniosynostosis, osteoblasts mineralize the suture before the completion of brain growth, alter subsequent growth patterns of cranial dermal bone, and produce abnormal head shapes.
source: In craniosynostosis, a condition that always involves premature fusion of cranial suture(s) and can include additional postcranial and craniofacial anomalies, osteoblasts mineralize the suture before the completion of brain growth, alter subsequent growth patterns of cranial dermal bone, and produce abnormal head shapes (Flaherty et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on craniosynostosis.

claim: Approximately 1 in 2000–2500 children of all ethnic groups are born with craniosynostosis conditions.
source: Approximately 1 in 2000–2500 children of all ethnic groups are born with craniosynostosis conditions (Heuzé et al., 2014; Lajeunie et al., 2006) and though variants of many genes are associated with these disorders (Cuellar et al., 2020; Calpena et al., 2020; Goos and Mathijssen, 2019; Holmes et al., 2021; Justice et al., 2012; Maruyama et al., 2021; Wilkie, 1997; Wilkie and Morriss-Kay, 2001), alteration to the function of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) results in the more common craniosynostosis syndromes of Apert, Crouzon, and Pfeiffer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published epidemiological literature.

claim: Alteration to the function of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) results in the more common craniosynostosis syndromes of Apert, Crouzon, and Pfeiffer.
source: Approximately 1 in 2000–2500 children of all ethnic groups are born with craniosynostosis conditions (Heuzé et al., 2014; Lajeunie et al., 2006) and though variants of many genes are associated with these disorders (Cuellar et al., 2020; Calpena et al., 2020; Goos and Mathijssen, 2019; Holmes et al., 2021; Justice et al., 2012; Maruyama et al., 2021; Wilkie, 1997; Wilkie and Morriss-Kay, 2001), alteration to the function of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) results in the more common craniosynostosis syndromes of Apert, Crouzon, and Pfeiffer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on craniosynostosis genetics.

claim: The distinctive set of non-sutural phenotypes that comprise each craniosynostosis syndrome depicts craniosynostosis as a complex growth disorder affecting multiple cranial tissues.
source: Though nearly all individuals affected with each of these syndromes have premature suture closure, the distinctive set of non-sutural phenotypes that comprise each syndrome depicts craniosynostosis as a complex growth disorder affecting multiple cranial tissues whose development is targeted by variants in ways that remain poorly understood (Flaherty et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and represents an inference about the nature of craniosynostosis.

claim: The Fgfr2cC342Y/+ Crouzon syndrome mouse model carries a cysteine to tyrosine substitution at amino acid 342 (Cys342Tyr; C342Y) in the protein encoded by Fgfr2c equivalent to the FGFR2 variant common to Pfeiffer and Crouzon syndromes.
source: The Fgfr2cC342Y/+ Crouzon syndrome mouse model (Eswarakumar et al., 2004) carries a cysteine to tyrosine substitution at amino acid 342 (Cys342Tyr; C342Y) in the protein encoded by Fgfr2c equivalent to the FGFR2 variant common to Pfeiffer and Crouzon syndromes (Eswarakumar et al., 2004; Oldridge et al., 1995; Reardon et al., 1994; Rutland et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the mouse model and human syndromes.

claim: The FGFR2c C342Y variant is associated with constitutive activation of the receptor that increases osteoblast proliferation.
source: The FGFR2c C342Y variant is associated with constitutive activation of the receptor that increases osteoblast proliferation (Eswarakumar et al., 2004), may affect osteoblast differentiation at different stages of development (Liu et al., 2013; Miraoui et al., 2009), and is associated with craniofacial dysmorphogenesis and premature fusion of the coronal suture, typically prenatally.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on the molecular effects of the variant.

claim: The FGFR2c C342Y variant may affect osteoblast differentiation at different stages of development.
source: The FGFR2c C342Y variant is associated with constitutive activation of the receptor that increases osteoblast proliferation (Eswarakumar et al., 2004), may affect osteoblast differentiation at different stages of development (Liu et al., 2013; Miraoui et al., 2009), and is associated with craniofacial dysmorphogenesis and premature fusion of the coronal suture, typically prenatally.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and is stated as a possibility.

claim: The FGFR2c C342Y variant is associated with craniofacial dysmorphogenesis and premature fusion of the coronal suture, typically prenatally.
source: The FGFR2c C342Y variant is associated with constitutive activation of the receptor that increases osteoblast proliferation (Eswarakumar et al., 2004), may affect osteoblast differentiation at different stages of development (Liu et al., 2013; Miraoui et al., 2009), and is associated with craniofacial dysmorphogenesis and premature fusion of the coronal suture, typically prenatally.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on the phenotypic effects of the variant.

claim: In mice, Fgfr2c is required for normal function of osteoblast lineage cells.
source: In mice, Fgfr2c is required for normal function of osteoblast lineage cells and interacts with Fgfr3, important to cells in the chondrocyte lineage during endochondral osteogenesis (Eswarakumar et al., 2004; Eswarakumar et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on Fgfr2c function.

claim: Fgfr2c interacts with Fgfr3, important to cells in the chondrocyte lineage during endochondral osteogenesis.
source: In mice, Fgfr2c is required for normal function of osteoblast lineage cells and interacts with Fgfr3, important to cells in the chondrocyte lineage during endochondral osteogenesis (Eswarakumar et al., 2004; Eswarakumar et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on Fgfr interactions.

claim: The established explanation for cranial dysmorphogenesis in craniosynostosis syndromes is that premature closure of sutures results in changes in growth trajectories local to sutures of the growing skull.
source: The established explanation for cranial dysmorphogenesis in craniosynostosis syndromes is that premature closure of sutures results in changes in growth trajectories local to sutures of the growing skull (Johnson and Wilkie, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature describing the prevailing hypothesis.

claim: Skulls of mice carrying specific Fgfr2 variants are dysmorphic prior to suture closure.
source: However, skulls of mice carrying specific Fgfr2 variants are dysmorphic prior to suture closure (Motch Perrine et al., 2014), cranial tissues other than bone are dysmorphic in these mice at birth (Holmes et al., 2018; Martínez-Abadías et al., 2013; Motch Perrine et al., 2017; Peskett et al., 2017), and a diversity of cell types are identified within the embryonic murine coronal suture by single cell transcriptome analysis (Farmer et al., 2021; Holmes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cranial tissues other than bone are dysmorphic in mice carrying specific Fgfr2 variants at birth.
source: However, skulls of mice carrying specific Fgfr2 variants are dysmorphic prior to suture closure (Motch Perrine et al., 2014), cranial tissues other than bone are dysmorphic in these mice at birth (Holmes et al., 2018; Martínez-Abadías et al., 2013; Motch Perrine et al., 2017; Peskett et al., 2017), and a diversity of cell types are identified within the embryonic murine coronal suture by single cell transcriptome analysis (Farmer et al., 2021; Holmes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A diversity of cell types are identified within the embryonic murine coronal suture by single cell transcriptome analysis.
source: However, skulls of mice carrying specific Fgfr2 variants are dysmorphic prior to suture closure (Motch Perrine et al., 2014), cranial tissues other than bone are dysmorphic in these mice at birth (Holmes et al., 2018; Martínez-Abadías et al., 2013; Motch Perrine et al., 2017; Peskett et al., 2017), and a diversity of cell types are identified within the embryonic murine coronal suture by single cell transcriptome analysis (Farmer et al., 2021; Holmes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The unique capacity of cartilage to grow interstitially enables rapid, continuous growth in size and change in shape ensuring customized protection for embryonic cranial organs prior to bone formation.
source: The unique capacity of cartilage to grow interstitially enabling rapid, continuous growth in size and change in shape ensures customized protection for embryonic cranial organs prior to bone formation, and the established association between cranial cartilage and endochondral bone confirms the importance of chondrocranial elements to skull shape.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of cartilage biology.

claim: The established association between cranial cartilage and endochondral bone confirms the importance of chondrocranial elements to skull shape.
source: The unique capacity of cartilage to grow interstitially enabling rapid, continuous growth in size and change in shape ensures customized protection for embryonic cranial organs prior to bone formation, and the established association between cranial cartilage and endochondral bone confirms the importance of chondrocranial elements to skull shape.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and represents an inference about the functional importance of the chondrocranium.

claim: The demonstrated temporospatial association between specific cranial cartilages and individual dermal bones during embryogenesis suggests the potential for the chondrocranium to influence the position, size, shape, and development of dermal bones.
source: Though not as extensively studied, the demonstrated temporospatial association between specific cranial cartilages and individual dermal bones during embryogenesis (Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017a; Pitirri et al., 2020) suggests the potential for the chondrocranium to influence the position, size, shape, and development of dermal bones.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and represents an inference about the functional significance of the association.

claim: The prenatal dermatocranium is dysmorphic in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice.
source: Since it is known that the prenatal dermatocranium is dysmorphic in these mice, three outcomes are possible: (i) chondrocranial morphology of Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice and their controls (Fgfr2c+/+ littermates) is similar indicating that the variant affects the cranial osteoblast lineage but not the chondrocyte series; (ii) chondrocranial morphology separates Fgfr2cC342Y/+ and Fgfr2c+/+ littermates but there is a lack of correspondence in the morphological effects on the dermatocranium and the chondrocranium indicating that the variant affects the chondrocyte series and the osteoblast lineage but that the two cranial skeletons are dissociated; or (iii) chondrocranial morphology differs between genotypes and the morphological effects of the variant on chondrocranial cartilages and dermatocranial bone show correspondence, indicating integration of chondrocranial and dermatocranial development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the mouse model.

claim: The Fgfr2c C342Y mutation induces changes in chondrocranial cartilages that in turn, affect the development of cranial dermal bone.
source: Our quantitative analyses demonstrate that the Fgfr2c C342Y mutation induces changes in chondrocranial cartilages that in turn, affect the development of cranial dermal bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Embryonic bone was segmented from 3D micro-computed tomography (microCT) images by thresholding techniques using Avizo 2020.2.
source: Embryonic bone was segmented from 3D micro-computed tomography (microCT) images by thresholding techniques using Avizo 2020.2 (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA), but segmenting embryonic cranial cartilage using deep learning based fully convolutional networks (FCNs) (Long et al., 2015; Ronneberger et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2019) remains a challenging task.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the study.

claim: Segmenting embryonic cranial cartilage using deep learning based fully convolutional networks (FCNs) remains a challenging task.
source: Embryonic bone was segmented from 3D micro-computed tomography (microCT) images by thresholding techniques using Avizo 2020.2 (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA), but segmenting embryonic cranial cartilage using deep learning based fully convolutional networks (FCNs) (Long et al., 2015; Ronneberger et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2019) remains a challenging task.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical challenges in the field, supported by citations.

claim: A new two-phase approach implementing sparse annotation was used for training the segmentation model.
source: Consequently, a new two-phase approach implementing sparse annotation was used for training our segmentation model.
evidence: This is a description of the novel method developed for the study.

claim: The two-phase approach produced full 3D reconstructions of the chondrocranium from E13.5 through E17.5 for Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice and their Fgfr2c+/+ littermates.
source: Our two-phase approach (https://github.com/ndcse-medical/CartSeg_UGST; Sapkota, 2022) is built on an automatic segmentation procedure (Zheng et al., 2020) that produced full 3D reconstructions of the chondrocranium from E13.5 through E17.5 for Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice and their Fgfr2c+/+ littermates (Figure 1; Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described and the resulting data shown in Figure 1.

claim: At E15.5, the Fgfr2c+/+ mouse chondrocranium is complete, consisting of the olfactory region, braincase floor, and lateral walls of the preoccipital and occipital regions.
source: (A, B) At embryonic day 15.5 (E15.5), the Fgfr2c+/+ mouse chondrocranium, (A) lateral, and (B) superior views is complete, consisting of the olfactory region, braincase floor, and lateral walls of the preoccipital and occipital regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description and visualization in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The appearance of the parachordal cartilages marks the initiation of the chondrocranium in C57BL/6 J mice at E12.5.
source: The appearance of the parachordal cartilages marks the initiation of the chondrocranium in C57BL/6 J mice at E12.5 (Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017a; Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017b) with the subsequent appearance and continual growth of additional chondrocranial cartilages (Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017a; Pitirri et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: By E13.5, the lateral wall of the preoccipital region of Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice consists of well-developed ala orbitalis (AO), sphenethmoid commissure (CSE), and tectum transversum (TTR), while Fgfr2c+/+ mice do not adequately develop these structures until E14.5.
source: By E13.5, the lateral wall of the preoccipital region of Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice consists of well-developed ala orbitalis (AO), sphenethmoid commissure (CSE), and tectum transversum (TTR), while Fgfr2c+/+ mice do not adequately develop these structures until E14.5 (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; see https://doi.org/10.25550/J-RHCA for interactive viewer of 3D reconstructions).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from 3D reconstructions shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The tectum nasi (TN), AO, and TTR are more developed and thicker in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice relative to Fgfr2c+/+ mice at E13.5, as shown by 3D thickness maps and cleared and stained specimens.
source: The tectum nasi (TN), AO, and TTR are more developed and thicker in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice relative to Fgfr2c+/+ mice at E13.5, as shown by 3D thickness maps (Figure 2A and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and cleared and stained specimens (Figure 2B and C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E13.5, Fgfr2cC342Y/+ and Fgfr2c+/+ mice show a break in the brain case floor between the septum nasi (SN) and the hypophysis.
source: At E13.5, Fgfr2cC342Y/+ and Fgfr2c+/+ mice show a break in the brain case floor between the septum nasi (SN) and the hypophysis (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from figures.

claim: At E13.5, the AO and TTR extend further apically over the developing brain and are larger in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice relative to Fgfr2c+/+ mice.
source: At E13.5, the AO and TTR extend further apically over the developing brain and are larger in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice relative to Fgfr2c+/+ mice, and the portion of the orbitoparietal commissure (COP) rostral to the TTR contains relatively more cartilage along its apical lip (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from figures.

claim: From E14.5 through E17.5, the AO and TTR appear thicker and extend more apically in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ relative to Fgfr2c+/+ mice.
source: From E14.5 through E17.5, the AO and TTR appear thicker and extend more apically in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ relative to Fgfr2c+/+ mice, with more apical projections of thin parietal plate (PP) cartilage over time, even as skull bone mineralizes (Figure 2B and C; Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from Figure 2 and its supplements.

claim: Most elements of the chondrocranium have formed by E15.5.
source: Most elements of the chondrocranium have formed by E15.5 (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from figures.

claim: Endochondral ossification has not yet initiated at E15.5 and dermatocranial elements are just beginning to form so the E15.5 skull is predominantly cartilaginous.
source: Endochondral ossification has not yet initiated at this age and dermatocranial elements are just beginning to form so the E15.5 skull is predominantly cartilaginous (Figure 1—video 1, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from video figures.

claim: Disintegration of portions of the chondrocranium is not evident at E15.5 but prior to E16.5, AO, TTR, and COP begin to dissolve in both genotypes.
source: Disintegration of portions of the chondrocranium is not evident at E15.5 but prior to E16.5, AO, TTR, and COP begin to dissolve in both genotypes, becoming thinner and taking on a lace-like appearance (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from figures.

claim: At E17.5, cartilages of the Fgfr2cC342Y/+ chondrocrania remain more complete relative to Fgfr2c+/+ mice.
source: Though cartilage is disappearing in both genotypes at E17.5, cartilages of the Fgfr2cC342Y/+ chondrocrania remain more complete relative to Fgfr2c+/+ mice (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 5; Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from figures.

claim: After E17.5, additional parts of the chondrocranium begin or continue to thin and disappear in both genotypes as the dermatocranium thickens and expands.
source: After E17.5, additional parts of the chondrocranium begin or continue to thin and disappear in both genotypes as the dermatocranium thickens and expands.
evidence: This is an observation about the developmental progression.

claim: Chondrocyte proliferation, hypertrophy, and matrix deposition are the cellular processes that contribute to cartilage growth in long bones.
source: Observations of growth plate cartilages in long bones identify chondrocyte proliferation, hypertrophy, and matrix deposition as the cellular processes that contribute to cartilage growth (Breur et al., 1991; Cooper et al., 2013; Wilsman et al., 2008) while Kaucka and colleagues (Kaucka et al., 2017) proposed oriented clonal cell dynamics as the basis for accurate shaping of nasal cartilages.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on cartilage biology.

claim: Oriented clonal cell dynamics is proposed as the basis for accurate shaping of nasal cartilages.
source: Observations of growth plate cartilages in long bones identify chondrocyte proliferation, hypertrophy, and matrix deposition as the cellular processes that contribute to cartilage growth (Breur et al., 1991; Cooper et al., 2013; Wilsman et al., 2008) while Kaucka and colleagues (Kaucka et al., 2017) proposed oriented clonal cell dynamics as the basis for accurate shaping of nasal cartilages.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: There are significantly more chondrocytes in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ septum nasi at E14.5 and E16.5 relative to Fgfr2c+/+ mice.
source: We found significantly more chondrocytes in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ SN at E14.5 (p=0.006) and E16.5 (p≤0.001) relative to Fgfr2c+/+ littermates (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Chondrocytes in the septum nasi were larger in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice at E13.5 and E16.5.
source: Chondrocytes in the septum nasi were larger in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice at E13.5 (p=0.004) and E16.5 (p=0.016) (Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The amount of matrix within the septum nasi was increased at E14.5 in Fgfr2cC342Y/+ mice relative to Fgfr2c+/+ littermates.

claim: There exist interspecies differences in the cartilages that compose the chondrocranium.
source: Though in our experience the relationship between specific chondrocranial cartilages and dermal bones is constant across mouse strains, there exist interspecies differences in the cartilages that compose the chondrocranium (de Beer, 1937), and the association of chondrocranial elements with specific dermal bones varies over time and across species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The association of chondrocranial elements with specific dermal bones varies over time and across species.

evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: Some cartilages of the mouse chondrocranium are not present in humans.
source: Some cartilages of the mouse chondrocranium are not present in humans for example (Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017a), and their function is most likely assumed by an alternate cartilage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The function of cartilages present in mice but not in humans is most likely assumed by an alternate cartilage.
source: Some cartilages of the mouse chondrocranium are not present in humans for example (Kawasaki and Richtsmeier, 2017a), and their function is most likely assumed by an alternate cartilage.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about functional equivalence.

claim: Though the link between the chondrocranium and dermatocranium is robust, the association between the two skeletal systems appears to have the ability to vary and can evolve.
source: Though the link between the chondrocranium and dermatocranium is robust, the association between the two skeletal systems appears to have the ability to vary and can evolve, with the potential for differing signaling systems to direct these links in different species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary flexibility of the chondrocranium-dermatocranium relationship.
